chunks: "Characteristic impedance is the ratio of voltage to current for a wave traveling along a line.
If I put a step on the line, the wave front moves down at some speed, and as it goes it has to charge up the capacitance of each new bit of line and build up current through its inductance.
The current that has to flow to do that is set by how fast the front moves and how much capacitance there is per unit length.
Work through it and you get Z 0 equals square root of L' over C' , in ohms, with L' and C' the inductance and capacitance per unit length.
The key points: it depends only on the geometry and the dielectric, not on the length. A 1 m and a 10 m piece of the same coax are both 50 ohms.
It isn't a resistance in the sense that it doesn't dissipate power: a lossless line still has a Z 0 , and an ohmmeter can't measure it.
What it means is that until the wave comes back from the far end, the source sees the line as a resistor of value Z 0 .
That's why a driver launches V s Z 0 over (R s plus Z 0) , and why a load equal to Z 0 absorbs the wave with no reflection.
On a PCB I set it with the trace width, the dielectric thickness and the dielectric constant, and typically target 50 ohms single-ended or 100 differential."
